prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength allow optical-frequency timekeeping of unprecedented accuracy and stability

statement.case_for: I keep a single prize part for B040 with Katori and Ye, and my configuration is unchanged from round 1. The chair asks what the lattice clock adds beyond the 2005 and 2012 prizes. My one-sentence answer is this: the 2005 prize rewarded a spectroscopic tool (the comb) that reads out optical frequencies, and the 2012 prize rewarded control of single quantum systems, whereas the lattice clock is a new kind of clock, because the magic-wavelength condition lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be trapped without shifting the clock transition, and so combines the accuracy once reserved for single ions with the statistics of many atoms. That is a different physical idea with its own demonstrated performance, near 1e-18, reproduced and compared across independent laboratories. On the citation wording I prefer a species-neutral statement of the concept and the platform, with the invention and development of the clock as the object, because it avoids a priority dispute over strontium versus ytterbium and over who first reached which accuracy record. The pair is the most defensible credit: Katori for the concept and first realisation, Ye for taking the platform to the accuracy frontier. Nothing in the supplied material gives a stronger argument for a third name than the two-name credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest remaining objection is that a sceptical reader sees a third award in one precision-spectroscopy lineage after 2005 and 2012, and I cannot fully remove that reading; I can only say the citation must isolate the magic-wavelength lattice so that the answer is in the text. Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow, Takamoto and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups are real contributors left outside a two-name credit, and the three-laureate limit means the record cannot name them. The redefinition of the second and relativistic geodesy are partly prospective, so the citation should rest on the demonstrated invention and performance and not on those applications.

responses.point: Danielsson prefers B018 (Halzen and Karle) as a discovery of a new observational channel, a diffuse flux of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos, and treats B040 as the safer alternative if the committee wants maturity.
responses.response: I take the 'new channel' argument seriously and I do not dismiss IceCube: the diffuse flux is established and the instrument is remarkable. But the two points you yourself list as reservations weigh heavily for me. The dominant sources are unidentified, so a citation limited to the diffuse flux describes a detection without an interpretation, and a two-name credit sets aside AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND for a result obtained by a collaboration of hundreds. Your own case against says B040 is the safer choice if maturity decides, and I think it does. I have kept B018 as my first alternative because of your argument, but I do not think waiting on source identification is unfair to IceCube; it is the reason a later prize would be better grounded. I would ask whether you could accept B040 as the prize this year given that you list it first among your alternatives.

responses.point: Kroll answered my round-1 point on the redefinition of the second: demonstrated 1e-18 agreement between independent clocks is enough, whatever the metrological bodies decide, and a third name would need evidence from the supplied material.
responses.response: I accept that answer and withdraw the weight I gave to prospective impact as a maturity doubt: it is an application, and the comparisons already done establish the discovery. I also agree with you on the third name. Where I would still press is the disclosure you made about the Hall laboratory stay. Hall shares the 2005 prize that bounds B040, and you list the continuity reading in your own case against. I think a documented stay without a tie to Katori or Ye does not require recusal, but I would want the committee to record the decision and not leave it implicit, since the distinctness question is exactly where your background could be seen to matter. On the role split, I would not word the citation by dividing roles between Katori and Ye, because that invites the priority question the chair wants to avoid.

responses.point: Pearce asked whether I think the exact-solution contributors in B005 (KPZ) can be reconciled with a three-name limit, and holds B018 and B035 as fallbacks if B040 stalls.
responses.response: No. I considered it again and I do not see a three-name credit for KPZ that is fair to the exact-solution contributors, including Parisi and the later solvers, while also carrying the experimental confirmation by Takeuchi. Since you ask directly: I am not putting B005 forward. I disclosed proximity because it lies in my field and I do not want that field closeness to inflate its standing in my ranking. On your fallbacks, I would prefer B018 to B035 if B040 stalled, because Higgs observation cannot be reduced to three names without leaving out people with decisive roles, but I would not make that choice without the AMANDA, Baikal and DUMAND lineage being acknowledged.

responses.point: Olsson says the prize should reward a specific invention with a precisely stated principle, that the citation must rest on the demonstrated invention and not on the redefinition of the second, and that attribution should be two names.
responses.response: I agree on all three points, and the one-sentence principle in her citation (atoms confined at a magic wavelength allowing timekeeping at optical frequency) is close to the wording I would adopt. I would make two small changes: drop 'unprecedented' if the committee wants a citation that does not date, and keep the object as the invention and development of the clock so that Katori's concept and Ye's development are both inside the sentence without an explicit split. I also note, as a theorist outside atomic physics, that my own agreement should count for less than the judgement of Lindroth, who works in the field and called the two-name division clean.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 single-system prizes; I think it is distinct, but this is a judgement and not a computable fact.
The relative weight of Katori and Ye against Lemonde, Hollberg, Ludlow and the NIST, PTB and SYRTE groups is not settled by the supplied credit.
Whether Danielsson, who prefers B018, would accept B040, so I cannot tell whether the private vote will be unanimous.
Whether a theory-heavy second part such as B004 would be distinct enough and cleanly credited to be added to B040; I do not currently think the case is strong enough to justify a second part.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for B040, B018 or B004. My only disclosure remains scientific proximity to B005 (stochastic processes, random matrices), which I am no longer putting forward. None of my listed co-authors or institutions appear among the credited names. I note Kroll's Hall disclosure and think the committee should record its decision on it.
